title: Efficient fidelity simulation of high-rate magic distillation circuits
authors: Xiao Xiao, Dominik Hangleiter, J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides, Rohan Mehta, Varun Menon, Mikhail D. Lukin, Michael J. Gullans
abstract: Non-Clifford gates are essential for avoiding classical simulability under the Gottesman-Knill theorem. An error-corrected circuit with non-Clifford gates will therefore be an important element for realizing useful fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. However, accurately understanding the fault-tolerant performance of such circuits faces challenges due to the classical hardness of simulating these circuits. We avoid simulating logical measurements and develop exact and efficient classical methods for benchmarking circuits composed of X, CNOT, and diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, including state and gate teleportation gadgets with feedforward. For circuits with third-level diagonal gates, our benchmarking algorithm efficiently samples syndrome statistics and estimates the output logical fidelity and expectation values of certain Clifford observables, including all Pauli observables. The evaluation of syndrome expectation values also extends to circuits with fourth-level diagonal gates. Our algorithm scales polynomially in the number of physical qubits n and circuit depth T, independent of the number of logical qubits. The benchmarking applications include IQP sampling and magic state preparation/cultivation. We demonstrate the practical utility of our simulation algorithms by using them to optimize high-rate magic state distillation factories based on three copies of a [[27,3,3]] tricycle code.
summary: This paper presents efficient classical simulation techniques to benchmark the fault-tolerant performance of quantum circuits involving non-Clifford gates. By focusing on syndrome sampling and observable expectation values rather than full simulation, the authors achieve polynomial scaling. This methodology is practically demonstrated by optimizing high-rate magic state distillation factories.
main_problem: Developing exact and efficient classical methods to benchmark the fault-tolerant performance of quantum circuits containing non-Clifford gates.
main_result: The developed algorithms scale polynomially in physical qubits and circuit depth, allowing for the optimization of high-rate magic state distillation factories.
method: The approach uses Monte Carlo methods to sample syndrome statistics and estimate logical fidelity and Pauli observable expectation values, avoiding full circuit simulation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on circuits composed of X, CNOT, and diagonal gates belonging to the Clifford hierarchy, particularly analyzing AD(3) and AD(4) circuits used in quantum error correction.
key_observables: Logical fidelity, expectation values of Pauli observables, and syndrome statistics.
important_parameters: Physical qubits (n), circuit depth (T), and the level of the diagonal gate ($\ell$).
main_assumptions: The efficiency relies on the structure of error propagation following a hierarchy reduction, and certain fidelity calculations assume ideal mapping between reference subspaces.
figures_summary: Figures compare computational cost scaling for fidelity estimation on hypercube-IQP circuits and compare infidelity vs. acceptance rate for different Z syndrome extraction protocols.
paper_structure: The paper develops general algorithms for syndrome sampling and observable estimation for AD($\ell$) circuits, applies these to IQP sampling, and demonstrates utility by optimizing magic state distillation using a [[27,3,3]] code.
why_interesting: The techniques developed for efficiently simulating fault-tolerant circuits are highly relevant for understanding the performance limits of quantum computation hardware.

Black circles: one-time precomputation (simulator con- struction, back-propagation of faults and measured sta- bilizers, and the fault–measurement commutator tables), with a fitted power law n2.51 (dashed). Blue squares: cost per Monte-Carlo sample, obtained by subtracting the precomputation from the total run time and divid- ing by the number of samples. No power law is quoted for the latter because its local slope still rises across this range (1.3 →2.3). See Section S4.3 for the scaling of the individual subroutines.
